extracted.intended_audience: communications professionals, PR and measurement practitioners, evaluators, and communicators in corporate, government, NGO/charity sectors
extracted.subtask_description: High-level industry principles (Barcelona Principles 3.0) for planning, measuring, and evaluating communications and PR work, applicable across commercial, government, and non-profit organisations. Emphasises goal-setting, outcomes/impact, mixed methods, channel-agnostic measurement, and integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setting goals is an absolute prerequisite to communications planning, measurement, and evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: The founding principle of SMART (specific, measurable, actionable, relevant, and time-bound) goals is promoted to an essential prerequisite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This elevates measurement and evaluation as a core component of the planning process: goals should articulate target outcomes and how progress towards them will be assessed. SMART goals form the foundation for communications planning, measurement, and evaluation; without clear goals, measurement cannot be meaningfully aligned to outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement and evaluation should identify outputs, outcomes, and potential impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Measurement should move beyond counting outputs to identify outcomes and consider longer-term impact of communications strategy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The update extends the previous recommendation (measure outcomes rather than simply counting outputs) to also consider potential longer-term impact. Practitioners should think about the channels they are impacting and the change they wish to see through campaigns, events and activations, not just short-term or immediate metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcomes and impact should be identified for stakeholders, society, and the organization
rubrics_metrics.description: Outcomes and impact must be defined across multiple beneficiaries: stakeholders, society at large, and the organisation itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This broadens the focus from business-only metrics (e.g., sales, revenue) to a more holistic view of performance, making the model relevant to government communications, charities, NGOs and other non-commercial entities. Define and measure outcomes/impact that matter to each of these audiences where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication measurement and evaluation should include both qualitative and quantitative analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the full suite of methods — both qualitative and quantitative — to understand the full impact of communications work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantitative measures alone are insufficient; qualitative analysis is required to understand how messages are being received, believed, and interpreted. Employ mixed-method approaches to capture both extent and meaning of impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: AVEs are not the value of communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertising Value Equivalents (AVEs) do not demonstrate the value of communications work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AMEC’s position remains that AVEs are not a valid measure of value. Communicators should employ richer, more nuanced, and multi-faceted approaches to demonstrate value and impact instead of relying on AVEs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Holistic communication measurement and evaluation includes all relevant online and offline channels
rubrics_metrics.description: All relevant online and offline channels should be measured and evaluated equally, including earned, owned, shared, and paid channels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The principle reflects the shift in social communications capabilities and influence: social media can and should be measured. The AMEC measurement framework promotes clarity across channel types to ensure consistency in approach toward a common goal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication measurement and evaluation are rooted in integrity and transparency to drive learning and insights
rubrics_metrics.description: Measurement practices must prioritise integrity and transparency, enabling learning and the application of insights back into planning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrity and transparency are essential in light of data privacy and stewardship (e.g., GDPR). Measurement should go beyond data collection/tracking to learning from evaluation and applying insights into communications planning. Be transparent about programme context and aware of biases in tools, methodologies, and interpretation.
